messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Interior Designer
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 57

He was forty-three when they came for him. A Thursday afternoon, the kind of humid, slow-moving day that made time feel like it might stop. He was walking home from a job site – a beachfront villa he was helping a client renovate, choosing wood finishes that would hold up against salt and sun. He remembers the heat, the smell of frangipani mixing with exhaust from a passing truck. Then the truck stopped. The men inside wore uniforms he didn’t recognize, but their faces were familiar enough: hard, tired, bored. They pulled him in before he could react. The door slammed. That was the last sunlight he saw for four hundred and thirteen days.

He tells this story in fragments, over several sessions. He arranges the details the way he once arranged furniture – slowly, deliberately, leaving space. The cell was roughly the size of a walk-in closet, which he finds bitterly ironic now. He spent most of his career thinking about how to make small spaces feel open, how to use mirrors and light to trick the eye. The cell had neither. It had a concrete floor, a bucket, and a single bulb that burned day and night. He lost track of time faster than he expected. He counted breaths, then bricks in the wall, then the number of times the guard changed – at least that gave him a rhythm. But the noise kept him raw: the scrape of boots, the rattle of a chain, the distant sounds of others being questioned, crying, or going silent.

They wanted information he didn’t have. Or maybe they just wanted to break him. He was released in a prisoner swap, thin and hollow-eyed, but alive. He never learned why he was taken. The official explanation was a mistake, a case of mistaken identity. He still doesn’t believe it.

When he came home, his wife was waiting. She held him for a long time without speaking. For a while, he tried to go back to work. But the first client meeting was in a windowless conference room, and he couldn’t breathe. He excused himself, walked outside, and stood in the parking lot until his hands stopped shaking. He started avoiding small rooms altogether. He took only jobs that involved open-plan living, floor-to-ceiling windows, wraparound verandas. He became known for his light-filled spaces. Clients praised his sensitivity to natural light and flow. They didn’t know he was designing against the memory of a concrete box.

His wife died eight years ago. Cancer. He was with her at the end, in a hospital room that was small and white and smelled of antiseptic. He stayed for three days without leaving, even though the walls seemed to contract every time the door closed. He didn’t tell anyone that it was the hardest thing he had ever done – not because of the grief, but because the room was so much like the cell. He thought he was past that. He wasn’t.

Now he lives alone in a house he designed himself, open in every direction, with sliding glass doors that let the breeze through. He wakes at three or four in the morning, every morning, because that was when the guard used to make his rounds. He lies still, listening. His heart pounds. He knows he is safe. He tells himself this. It doesn’t matter. The fear lives in his body now, a kind of second skeleton. He checks the locks twice before bed. He arranges his furniture so no chair faces away from the door. He never takes on clients who want basements or windowless studies, even if the money is good. He doesn’t explain why. He just says it’s not his style.

He still works. It’s the only time he feels close to something like peace – when he’s choosing fabrics, matching colors, imagining a room that could hold a family’s whole life without suffocating them. Sometimes a client asks for wall-to-wall carpeting, and his stomach turns. He remembers the feel of damp concrete on his cheek. He says he prefers hardwood, offers a discount, and the client usually agrees. He never tells them why.

He has stopped attending social gatherings. Friends from before – from that other life – call occasionally. He lets the phone ring. He prefers the company of his work: swatches, blueprints, the clean line of a wall he can open to the sky. He is seventy-two years old, and he has spent nearly thirty years trying to make spaces that feel like freedom. But at night, in the dark, the cell returns. He doesn’t sleep. He waits for the sound of boots.
